extracted.intended_audience: general readers (especially young people/young men) seeking practical moral, financial, and health advice
extracted.subtask_description: Eighteenth-century practical guidance for gaining wealth, maintaining health, and cultivating virtuous habits — aimed at individuals seeking to improve fortune, reputation, and wellbeing through industry, frugality, and probity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctual payment and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The good paymaster is lord of another man's purse; punctuality and justice in all dealings raise a young man's standing and ability to borrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never keep borrowed money an hour beyond the time you promised; punctual payment enables one to 'raise all the money his friends can spare.' Small signs (working early/late rather than frequenting taverns) influence creditors' willingness to extend credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to trifling actions that affect credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Seemingly small behaviors influence creditors' confidence and therefore your credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noisy or idle habits (e.g., the sound of a hammer at inappropriate hours vs. seeing you at a billiard-table or tavern) change a creditor's view; appear mindful of what you owe to seem careful and honest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep exact accounts; distinguish credit from ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent thinking all you possess is truly yours by keeping exact accounts of expenses and income for some time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record particulars to discover how small expenses mount up and to identify future savings achievable without great inconvenience; this prevents living beyond what you truly own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry and frugality as the foundation of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The way to wealth depends chiefly on two words, industry and frugality: waste neither time nor money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He that gets all he can honestly, and saves all he gets (necessary expenses excepted), will certainly become rich (unless providence otherwise decides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet proportioned to constitution and activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Eat and drink such an exact quantity as the constitution of thy body allows in reference to the services of the mind or body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who study much should eat less than those who work hard; keep quantity and quality constant; avoid excess; adjust for youth, age, sickness, and differing complexions; eat for necessity, not pleasure; bring appetite to reason for long life and a vigorous mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving too much for trivial pleasures ('whistles')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overvalue or sacrifice important things for small or vain objects — 'Don't give too much for the whistle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'whistle' is a metaphor for trifles that tempt people to sacrifice time, liberty, virtue, friends, health, fortune, or reputation (examples: court favour, popularity, miserliness, sensual pleasure, appearance). Use the whistle anecdote to remember to economize against frivolous purchases or pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luxury can spur industry but also has costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury (taken as unnecessary expense) may be both a spur to labor and a public/private evil depending on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether laws can prevent unnecessary expense; a small local luxury can stimulate productive industry (e.g., demand for caps led to knitting mittens for sale). But exporting necessaries to import superfluities can be harmful to a nation's welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer useful labor over idleness or unproductive occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth's first elements come from labour producing necessaries and conveniences; many are employed in works that produce neither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ people in productive tasks (spinning, building, agriculture) rather than in entertainment or superfluities that consume necessaries without producing lasting value; large-scale shifts toward raising necessaries could support more people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value truthfulness; avoid lying in trade and life
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is the companion of the gods and foundational to justice, policy, credit, and social trust; falsehood is despicable and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honest dealers raise credit and customer loyalty; liars may gain short-term advantage but lose reputation and can become dangerous (e.g., perjury). Truth facilitates easy testimony and repeatable facts; lying leads to shame and social exclusion. In trade, avoid 'historical' (lying) practices even if useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small wastes of time and money compound into large losses
rubrics_metrics.description: Wasting a little money or time daily accumulates into significant loss over years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: wasting a groat a day equals over six pounds a year; wasting five shillings' worth of time is equivalent to losing five shillings; repeated small losses forgo the potential gains from investing or using that money. 'A penny saved is twopence clear.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ready money (cash) to buying on credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Buying on credit leads sellers to charge an advance to cover bad debts, so cash buyers escape that charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who pay ready money may avoid a general five percent advance charged by sellers who expect some losses from credit; buyers on credit effectively pay interest and the seller's share of bad-debt costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two simple rules to build and keep money
rubrics_metrics.description: First, let honesty and industry be constant companions; second, spend one penny less than thy clear gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following these rules leads to independence and prevents want; even small consistent saving ('a penny less') and steady honest industry compound into security and dignity regardless of absolute wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a grateful, positive disposition to increase happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: People who focus on conveniences and pleasant aspects of life become happy; those who fix on contraries become discontented and disliked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If habitually critical and fault-finding, one brings real social and personal harms; cure the habit by noticing and appreciating the 'handsome leg' (the good) rather than obsessing on the 'deformed leg' (the faults). This improves social standing and prospects.
